title: The Dream of the 1990s Is Alive Again in Cybersecurity | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z GP Zane Lackey argues AI (starting with Opus 4.5/4.6) has collapsed the cost of offense, returning cybersecurity to a 1990s/2000s-style era of frequent critical vulnerabilities, returning (now monetized) worms and a patching crisis. Defenders must test continuously, rebuild defense in depth around machine-speed detection, and reboot endpoint, identity and supply-chain security with AI-native vendors such as Neo, Keycard and Socket.

themes.theme: AI collapses the economics of offense

insights.claim: Zane Lackey (a16z) argues the Opus 4.5/4.6 models marked the start of a radical shift in offensive cyber economics, making vulnerability discovery and exploitation orders of magnitude faster, cheaper and more repeatable.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Frontier-model capability jumps directly expand attacker capacity; watch model releases as leading indicators for vuln-disclosure and breach volume.
insights.quote: Opus 4.5/4.6 marked the beginning of a radical change in the economics of offense.

insights.claim: AI-driven vulnerability discovery is surfacing serious bugs in key software packages that had been heavily audited for two decades and were assumed to be safe.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Assumptions that mature, audited infrastructure is low-risk are breaking; legacy software exposure is a rising enterprise liability.
insights.quote: key software packages that have been audited to death over the past couple decades (or so we thought)

insights.claim: Security teams report that emergency-level vulnerabilities, once rare events every several years, became the normal operating cadence for most of 2026, echoing the 1990s/2000s era when foundational software like Apache, OpenSSH, OpenSSL and BIND all had serious remote vulnerabilities in 2002 alone.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Incident-response load is structurally higher; demand for security tooling and services that reduce response time should rise.

insights.claim: Defenders now must worry about both zero-days (newly AI-discovered bugs) and '550-days' (long-known unpatched vulnerabilities) at the same time, whereas historically old unpatched bugs caused most breaches.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Budgets must cover both novel-vuln detection and basic patch hygiene; vendors addressing either end benefit.
insights.quote: we have to worry about vulnerabilities at both ends of the time spectrum, both zero-days and 550-days
insights.locator: There’s historically been a running joke

insights.claim: Virtually every security leader a16z speaks with expects a deluge of newly published vulnerabilities over the next several years, with the time from discovery to working exploit to active attack campaign continuing to collapse, producing more headline breaches.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Expect rising breach frequency and security spending; positions favoring cyber vendors and cyber-insurance repricing.

insights.claim: Lackey predicts self-propagating Internet worms, largely dormant since the late 2000s, will return because AI slashes exploit development time while enterprise patching timelines have not caught up.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Worm-scale incidents imply correlated, systemic cyber losses — relevant for cyber insurers and network-security vendors.
insights.quote: As AI wildly decreases vulnerability discovery and exploit development time, but patching timelines haven’t caught up yet, we will see windows of opportunity for Internet worms to make a return.

insights.claim: Unlike early-2000s worms such as SQLSlammer and Sasser that mostly sought self-propagation, new worms will be commercially motivated: stealing API keys, deploying ransomware and similar payloads.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Worm payloads targeting monetizable assets raise per-incident loss severity versus the nuisance worms of the past.

insights.claim: Stealing API keys to consume AI inference is rapidly displacing crypto mining as attackers' preferred use of stolen compute resources.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Inference-key theft is a new fraud vector for AI labs and API platforms; secrets management and key-abuse detection become more valuable; marginal decline in illicit crypto-mining demand.
insights.quote: stealing API keys for inference which is rapidly displacing crypto mining as the action of choice for attackers when using stolen resources

insights.claim: Worms faded in the late 2000s because key parts of the Microsoft ecosystem hardened and stopped having many remotely exploitable vulnerabilities, implying that attack waves recede once foundational software is secured.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests the current wave is a multi-year cycle that ends with hardened platforms — investment window favors those building the hardening.

insights.claim: The AI-era version of the Windows XP 'compromised before updates finish' problem now applies across the whole enterprise software ecosystem, not only operating systems.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Unpatched exposure windows are shrinking toward zero; vendors enabling rapid update pipelines gain urgency.
insights.locator: 2. It’s the Windows XP patching problem

insights.claim: Enterprises historically avoided automatic software updates because breakage risk outweighed security risk; machine-speed AI offense will flip that calculus and push patching to orders of magnitude faster speeds.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Expect structural growth in patch-automation, testing and rollback tooling; update-related outages may rise as a side effect.
insights.quote: AI unlocking offense at machine speed will change the calculus here
insights.locator: Up until now, enterprises have held off

insights.claim: Fast enterprise patching is hard because the volume of software inside an enterprise is staggering and a large share of it is no longer actively maintained; a16z is excited about startups that help enterprises patch orders of magnitude faster.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Signals an a16z investment thesis in patch-velocity/remediation startups and unmaintained-software support.
insights.locator: Secondly, because it’s a much harder problem

themes.theme: Hardened infrastructure as a product category

insights.claim: A new generation of products is expected whose core promise is delivering highly hardened versions of critical infrastructure components for enterprise use, echoing OpenBSD's security-first identity in the prior vulnerability era.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Watch for startups selling hardened/secure-by-default forks of core infrastructure; possible new enterprise category.

insights.claim: Previous generations of hardened-infrastructure businesses struggled commercially; whether today's security shift unlocks a significantly larger market for them remains an open question.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Treat the category with caution — historical TAM was small; validate demand before assuming the market has changed.
insights.quote: The previous generations of these had a hard time commercially
insights.locator: We will likely expect a new generation

insights.claim: Most security teams are shifting pentesting to be as continuous as possible and relegating legacy annual pentests to a compliance exercise.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Revenue shift from point-in-time pentest services to continuous/automated red-teaming platforms.

insights.claim: Legacy vulnerability management, scanning and pentesting are failing to find the issues behind current breaches; Lackey urges no-scope, full red-team testing with the latest attacker tools, plus aggressive internal testing because zero-days will make initial footholds easier.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Legacy vuln-scanning vendors face displacement risk; AI-native offensive-testing tools gain share.
insights.quote: Legacy approaches to vulnerability management, scanning, pentesting, etc. are simply not discovering the issues
insights.locator: For the era we are in

insights.claim: Attackers are using tools like Hinoki Security to access specialized post-trained security models that allow modern red-team testing without hitting model refusals.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Specialized refusal-free security models are a distinct market; general-model safety refusals push offensive users to niche providers.
insights.locator: For the era we are in

insights.claim: Defense in depth historically meant layering enough controls that one would work even if others were misconfigured or switched off; in the AI era even fully functioning controls will be bypassed by zero-days, new techniques and speed, so defense must shift to overlapping detection and AI-native-speed response.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Detection/response vendors that operate at machine speed should gain budget versus static preventive controls.
insights.quote: even if all your layers of controls are functioning correctly, the use of zero-days, new techniques, and outright speed will likely bypass one or more of your fully functioning controls

insights.claim: Historically attackers and defenders operated at roughly the same order of magnitude of speed, so slow layered defenses were tolerable; AI is breaking that parity.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Speed asymmetry is the core investable gap — tools closing time-to-detect/respond capture value.

insights.claim: The AI era requires a security-stack reboot comparable to the shift to cloud, when physical appliances gave way to cloud-native software controls, creating openings for new companies built from the ground up.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Platform shifts historically reset vendor leadership; incumbents in endpoint, identity and supply chain are exposed to AI-native entrants.

insights.claim: Endpoint security has entered a third generation, the agentic malware era, following the anti-virus era and the behavioral EDR era.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: EDR incumbents may face a generational transition similar to AV-to-EDR; a16z backs Neo for endpoint-native AI security.
insights.quote: we’ve now entered the third generation of malware and endpoint security which is the agentic malware era
insights.locator: The AI era changed virtually every part

insights.claim: Identity security must expand from authenticating and authorizing human actions to controlling how AI agents operate inside the enterprise, with Keycard positioned as the new Okta for agents.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Agent identity is an emerging category that could challenge Okta-style incumbents; Keycard is an a16z bet.
insights.quote: Keycard acting as the new Okta for agents

insights.claim: Open source supply-chain attacks have exploded because agentic coding pulls in ever more open source packages regardless of risk; Socket is cited as protecting organizations against this.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: Agentic coding adoption is a direct demand driver for software supply-chain security vendors.
insights.locator: In other areas like open source software supply chain

insights.claim: Lackey frames the current period as quite possibly the most extraordinary time to build in cybersecurity, as the crisis will unlock defensive capabilities that were previously a pipe dream.
insights.speaker: Zane Lackey
insights.so_what: a16z is leaning into cyber venture deployment; expect elevated startup formation and funding in AI-native security.
insights.quote: this quite possibly the most extraordinary time to be building in cybersecurity
insights.locator: While it may sound like unprecedented
